#+title: Agent skills
#+description: The skill as a construct in agent tooling: the SKILL.md format, its frontmatter, the invocation distinction, progressive disclosure, and how published collections organise their skills. Reference material about a format ORE Studio does not own.
#+type: knowledge
#+level: cross
#+filetags: :external:llm:claude_code:skills:reference:

* Summary

A *skill* in agent tooling is a document that an assistant loads to perform a
kind of work. The assistant is a [[id:0D919421-2B73-4322-9F79-9FDA38A67EA1][LLM]] driving a tool loop, and the properties of
that substrate, given externally on its own page, explain why the construct
exists: a model recalls its training unreliably and holds only what its context
window carries, so reusable know-how must be supplied as text it can read.
Anthropic defines the format for Claude Code: a directory holding a =SKILL.md=
file, whose frontmatter carries a name and a description, and whose body holds
the instructions the assistant follows. Other agent tools read the same format.

This page records the received notion and the conventions that have grown around
it. ORE Studio does not own the format. For the narrower definition this project
works to, see [[id:87D41A08-0B37-41CE-8483-B59B36BA87FA][The skill in the compass framework]].

* Detail

** The format

A skill is a directory. It contains a =SKILL.md= file and any supporting files
that file refers to. The frontmatter carries two required fields. The =name=
field gives the identifier a user types. The =description= field states what the
skill does and when to reach for it.

The body holds the instructions. Its length is not fixed by the format, and
published skills range from two lines to several hundred.

** Invocation

Published collections separate skills by who may invoke them. A *user-invoked*
skill runs only when a person types its name. A *model-invoked* skill may also
be reached by the assistant when the task matches its description. Claude Code
expresses the first with a =disable-model-invocation= flag.

The distinction matters because the description does different work in each
case. For a model-invoked skill the description is the trigger, and its wording
decides how reliably the skill fires. For a user-invoked skill the description
is documentation.

** Progressive disclosure

A skill body sits in the assistant's context whenever the skill runs. Long
bodies therefore cost attention. The common answer is to move material into
sibling files and refer to them from the body, so the assistant loads them only
when it needs them.

The technique has a cost of its own. Material behind a reference is reached only
if the referring sentence is worded well enough to trigger the read.
